cards.front: Define the QR decomposition of a matrix $A$.
cards.back: The QR decomposition expresses an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ as the product $A = QR$, where $Q$ is an $m \times m$ orthogonal matrix and $R$ is an $m \times n$ upper triangular matrix.

cards.front: What are the defining properties of $Q$ and $R$ in a QR decomposition $A=QR$?
cards.back: $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix, meaning its columns are orthonormal vectors and $Q^T Q = I$. If $Q$ is square, then $Q^{-1} = Q^T$. $R$ is an upper triangular matrix, meaning all entries below its main diagonal are zero ($R_{ij} = 0$ for $i > j$).

cards.front: Outline the steps to compute the QR decomposition of $A = [a_1 \dots a_n]$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.
cards.back:
1. For each column $a_j$ of $A$:
   a. Compute the orthogonal projection of $a_j$ onto the subspace spanned by the previously orthogonalized vectors $q_1, \dots, q_{j-1}$.
   b. Subtract this projection from $a_j$ to get an orthogonal vector $v_j$.
   c. Normalize $v_j$ to get $q_j = v_j / \|v_j\|$.
2. Form $Q = [q_1 \dots q_n]$.
3. Form $R$ such that $R_{ij} = q_i^T a_j$ for $i \le j$ and $R_{ij} = 0$ for $i > j$. Alternatively, $R = Q^T A$.

cards.front: How can QR decomposition be used to solve the linear least squares problem $Ax \approx b$?
cards.back:
1. Perform QR decomposition: $A = QR$.
2. Substitute into the normal equations: $(QR)^T (QR)x = (QR)^T b \implies R^T Q^T Q R x = R^T Q^T b$.
3. Since $Q^T Q = I$, this simplifies to $R^T R x = R^T Q^T b$.
4. If $A$ has full column rank, $R$ is invertible, so $R x = Q^T b$.
5. Solve $Rx = Q^T b$ for $x$ using back-substitution, as $R$ is upper triangular.

cards.front: Explain the core idea behind computing QR decomposition using Householder reflections.
cards.back: Householder reflections are orthogonal transformations (matrices $H$) that can zero out all elements below the first entry in a given vector. By applying a sequence of Householder reflections $H_k$ to $A$ from the left, we can systematically zero out elements below the main diagonal, transforming $A$ into an upper triangular matrix $R$. The product of these reflections, $H_n \dots H_1 A = R$, means $Q^T = H_n \dots H_1$, so $Q = (H_n \dots H_1)^T = H_1 \dots H_n$.

cards.front: Under what condition does a unique "reduced" QR decomposition $A=QR$ exist where $R$ has positive diagonal entries?
cards.back: A unique reduced QR decomposition exists if and only if the matrix $A$ has linearly independent columns (i.e., $A$ has full column rank). In this case, $A$ is $m \times n$ with $m \ge n$, $Q$ is $m \times n$ with orthonormal columns ($Q^T Q = I_n$), and $R$ is an $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries ($R_{ii} > 0$).

cards.front: Compare the numerical stability of Gram-Schmidt (classical vs. modified) and Householder reflections for QR decomposition.
cards.back:
• Classical Gram-Schmidt (CGS): Numerically unstable, especially for ill-conditioned matrices, leading to loss of orthogonality in $Q$.
  • Modified Gram-Schmidt (MGS): More stable than CGS, as it maintains orthogonality better by projecting against already orthogonalized vectors. Still less stable than Householder for very ill-conditioned problems.
  • Householder Reflections: Highly numerically stable. It is the preferred method in practice for its robustness in maintaining orthogonality and accuracy, even with ill-conditioned matrices.
